own_scenes.desc: La industria del pop surcoreano: artificioso, espectacular, reciclable y de alcance global. Su equivalente japonés es el J-pop.

notes.chapter: Loops 2 · Cap. 9: Gueto global: mutaciones de la música electrónica en la periferia de Occidente y la proliferación de escenas locales
notes.text: «Gangnam Style» de PSY (2012) fue el mayor éxito viral hasta «Despacito»: k-pop prefabricado en Seúl por S.M. Entertainment, YG y JYP (EXO, G-Dragon, BoA, Girls' Generation), con ritmos electro y riffs de trance holandés; sus equivalentes, c-pop y j-pop.

refs.q: una canción coreana firmada por un tal PSY
refs.para: Antes de que «Despacito» aterrizara en las plataformas de distribución online, el mayor éxito viral de la música moderna —tres mil millones de reproducciones en YouTube, y subiendo— había sido una canción coreana firmada por un tal PSY que, con el título de «Gangnam Style», parodiaba con sorna, pero aprovechándose de todos los recursos de hit-making ensayado durante décadas por la industria americana, uno de los fenómenos más estruendosos del entretenimiento comercial contemporáneo, el k-pop, una variedad de pop sintético y prefabricado que mueve a su alrededor una industria multimillonaria en la ciudad de Seúl. El k-pop es una excelente metáfora de la sociedad poscapitalista en la capital de Corea del Sur, la ciudad del mundo con mayor número de clínicas de cirugía estética por habitante y poblada por una masa adicta al retoque cosmético, la cultura de la imagen, la tecnología portátil y el selfie compulsivo: un tipo de pop que se entiende a partir del impacto directo y el artificio, producido en cadena y según una lógica de consumo desaforado, donde los productos obsoletos —o sea, los artistas ideados por un think tank con sede en el despacho de los grandes ejecutivos de los sellos dominantes— se retiran del mercado tan pronto como se estima que han pasado de moda o han producido su beneficio inmediato. El k-pop, con sus ritmos machacones, sus ganchos melódicos certeros y su diseño resplandeciente, es el equivalente musical al fast food ideado por cocineros con estrella Michelin o las colecciones de ropa de grandes cadenas con el sello de una diseñadora de larga carrera:…

podcast.title: Anticipated Hot 100 #1
podcast.body: It is considered "probably just a matter of time" before a K-Pop girl group achieves a top 10 or even a number one hit on the Hot 100, following in the footsteps of BTS. "It's probably just a matter of time before a Kpop Girl Group follows BTS into the top 10 or even to number 1 on the Hot 100."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: DMZ Propaganda Countermeasure
podcast.body: In South Korea, K-pop songs were blasted to the north from speakers set up along the south side of the demilitarized zone (DMZ). This was done to drown out propaganda announcements coming southward from North Korea, whose speakers were too weak to compete. The practice stopped in 2018 when it created too much tension and threatened hostilities. "In South Korea, speakers were set up along the south side of the demilitarized zone, and K-pop songs were blasted to the north."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Fan Army Chart Influence
podcast.body: K-pop, exemplified by "K-pop deities BTS" and their "BTS army," showcases a phenomenon where loyal fan armies actively contribute to number one debuts. These fandoms generate massive consumption through Spotify clicks and download purchases, effectively doing the record label's work to propel their heroes to the top of the charts. "these fan armies like the famed fandom of K-pop deities BTS, who are literally called the BTS army, will do the label's work for them."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: Toppermost of the Poppermost Edition Part 1

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: Toppermost of the Poppermost Edition Part 1

podcast.title: First K-Pop Act on Billboard 200 Album Chart
podcast.body: In 2014, the Korean quartet 2NE1 became the first K-Pop act to crack the top 100 on the Billboard 200 album chart, aided by their song "I Am The Best" being featured in an American ad campaign. "It helped make to anyone the first Kpop act to crack the top 100 on the Billboard 200 album chart."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: First Korean Artist on US Hot 100
podcast.body: In October 2009, the K-Pop quintet Wonder Girls made history when their song "Nobody" entered the Hot 100 at number 76, marking the first time a Korean artist appeared on the flagship US chart. "making it the first song by a Korean artist to appear on the flagship US chart, years before BTS or any Kpop boy band."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Frequent US Album Chart Toppers
podcast.body: A decade after BTS's breakthrough, K-Pop girl groups frequently top the US album chart. In 2022, BLACKPINK's "Born Pink" was the first by a Korean girl group to reach number one in America, and in summer 2023, NewJeans' EP "Get Up" also hit number one, edging out the "Barbie" soundtrack. "A decade later, after the breakthrough by BTS, Kpop Girl Groups frequently top the US album chart. In 2022, Blackpink's album Born Pink became the first by a Korean Girl Group to reach number 1 in America."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Global Reach via YouTube
podcast.body: K-pop, or Korean Pop, has achieved widespread global visibility thanks to YouTube's borderless platform. The ability for content to be legally monetized and accessible worldwide has allowed genres like K-pop to be seen "everywhere." "K-pop can be seen everywhere."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall and Future of the Music Video - Part 2

podcast.title: Growing Western Fanbase
podcast.body: K-Pop gradually attracted more Western fans, initially driven by girl groups like Girls' Generation. "Gradually, Kpop began to attract more Western fans, driven at first by Girl Groups like Korean Chart Commanders Girls Generation."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Merchandise Spending Habits
podcast.body: K-pop fans were found to spend the most on merchandise at shows compared to other genres. "K-pop fans spend the most."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Survey Says: Useful and Odd Music Surveys and Polls

podcast.title: Preference of Younger Generations
podcast.body: As emo's popularity waned during its decline (around 2008-2010), younger fans entering their coming-of-age years increasingly gravitated towards K-pop as a preferred musical genre. "Younger fans now in their coming of age years wanted something different, and for them that was pop, K-pop specifically, and hip-hop, so interest-wained."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Rise to Global Phenomenon (2010s)
podcast.body: The 2010s marked the rise of K-pop into a global phenomenon, representing the "next step in the globalization of music." Its rapid expansion and international success are expected to continue for decades. "The rise of K-pop into a global phenomenon. That's going to continue for decades to come. This has been nothing less than the next step in the globalization of music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the 2010s Part 5: Music and Tech
